entities.name: Temple of Faunus
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Temple of Faunus (Latin: Aedes Faunus), located on the Tiber Island (Insula Tiberina) in Rome, was an ancient Roman temple dedicated to Faunus, the Roman god of the forest, plains, and animals — the equivalent of the Greek god Pan — vowed and built following Roman military victories in the early 2nd century BCE. The Tiber Island location was significant: the island had long been associated with healing (it housed the Temple of Aesculapius, god of medicine) and with the intersection of natural forces through Rome's central river.

Faunus was among Rome's oldest italic deities, predating Greek religious influence. His festival, the Faunalia, was celebrated on February 13 and December 5 — rustic celebrations associated with shepherds, hunters, and agricultural workers rather than urban elites. The Temple of Faunus on the Tiber Island was vowed by the aediles Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus and Gaius Scribonius Curio following their victory in Sardinia (circa 194 BCE), with the funds derived from fines on people who had illegally grazed cattle on public lands — a fitting dedication given Faunus's pastoral associations.

The temple no longer survives above ground; its existence is known primarily from ancient literary sources including Ovid's Fasti and Roman historians. The Tiber Island today hosts the hospital of Fatebenefratelli, continuing the medical associations of the island since antiquity. The Temple of Faunus represents the persistence of pre-Greek Italic religious tradition within Rome's increasingly Hellenized religious culture.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Temple of Faunus — representing pre-Hellenistic Italic religious tradition, establishing pastoral deity worship on Rome's sacred Tiber Island, and documented in Ovid's Fasti — is a modest but historically informative example of Rome's layered religious geography.
